content: Uterine fibroids are non-cancerous tumors that develop from the smooth muscle cells of the uterus. Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) are compounds that interact with estrogen receptors, acting as estrogen in certain tissues while inhibiting estrogen activity in others. Numerous clinical studies have investigated the use of SERMs for the treatment of uterine fibroids, but their effectiveness remains a topic of debate. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and safety of SERMs in women diagnosed with uterine fibroids. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, PubMed, EMBASE, and several Chinese medical databases. Additional efforts included handsearching journals, reviewing reference lists, and exploring databases of ongoing trials and internet sources. These searches were performed in March and April of 2012. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared SERMs to other medical therapies, placebo, or no treatment in women aged 18 to 45 years with confirmed uterine fibroids. Data extraction and quality assessment were independently performed by two reviewers. Due to the heterogeneity of the identified studies, a meta-analysis was not conducted; instead, the findings were summarized narratively. Three studies, involving a total of 215 participants, met the inclusion criteria. The sample sizes of these trials ranged from 25 to 100 women. In all three studies, the SERM used was raloxifene. One study included the use of a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogue in both treatment groups. The comparison interventions across the studies included no treatment and placebo. Two of the three studies reported significant benefits from raloxifene, while the third study found no benefit at follow-up periods of three and six months. The overall quality of the evidence from these studies was rated as low or very low. All three studies reported adverse reactions, but the available data on these reactions were limited. The authors concluded that there is no consistent evidence from the limited number of studies to suggest that SERMs reduce the size of uterine fibroids or improve clinical outcomes. Further research is necessary to determine whether SERMs provide any therapeutic benefit for women with uterine fibroids. This updated review did not identify any new studies for inclusion.
